name: The Selfish Gene
statement: Look at evolution from the gene's point of view, and organisms are survival machines built to copy their genes.
statementAccent: organisms are survival machines built to copy their genes
meaning: The selfish gene is the gene-centred view of evolution, which holds that natural selection acts most fundamentally at the level of genes, the replicators that make copies of themselves across generations, and that organisms are survival machines, or vehicles, built by genes to propagate copies of those genes. The word selfish is a metaphor: a gene that, through its effects on the body, tends to promote its own replication will spread through a population, regardless of the consequences for the organism or the group. Popularised by Richard Dawkins in 1976, this view reframed the unit of selection and became one of the most influential, and most misread, ideas in modern biology.
mechanism: The framework distinguishes replicators, the genes that are faithfully copied and so can accumulate the effects of selection, from vehicles, or interactors, the bodies through which genes act on the world. Selection ultimately preserves or discards replicators according to the phenotypic effects they produce, so genes that build bodies and behaviours favouring their own transmission proliferate. This explains altruism through kin selection: a gene can spread by prompting an organism to help relatives who carry copies of the same gene. Dawkins extended the logic to the extended phenotype, in which a gene's reach spills beyond the body into the environment and other organisms.

examples.text: A gene disposing an animal to help close relatives can spread because those relatives carry copies of it, so the gene's-eye view accounts for cooperation without appeal to the good of the species.
Dawkins's 1982 extension, in which a beaver's dam or a parasite's manipulation of its host counts as a phenotypic effect of genes reaching outside the body that carries them.
Dawkins coined the word meme in the same 1976 book, as a unit of cultural transmission analogous to the gene, subject to its own selection.

variants.name: Replicators and vehicles
variants.text: Dawkins's distinction between the gene as replicator and the organism as vehicle, later refined by the philosopher David Hull, who preferred the term interactor for the entity that meets the environment.

variants.name: Multilevel selection
variants.text: The rival framing of David Sloan Wilson and Elliott Sober, in which selection acts at several levels including the group, offered as an alternative to strict gene-centrism.

whyItMatters: The selfish gene gave a vivid, unifying language to the gene-centred view of evolution and made a generation of biologists and readers think in terms of replicators, vehicles, and inclusive fitness. It clarified how altruism and cooperation can evolve through ordinary selection, popularised the extended phenotype, and even launched the study of memes and cultural evolution.

working.text: ask what effects would help a gene copy itself, and expect those genes, and the traits they build, to spread.
distinguish the gene that is copied from the body through which it acts, since selection ultimately preserves replicators.
take selfish to describe a gene's tendency to promote its own transmission, not selfish behaviour in organisms, which the view often explains as cooperation.

limits: The gene-centred view sits at the heart of the contested debate over the units and levels of selection, with critics arguing that selection acts on whole organisms or groups, not genes alone. Multilevel selection theory offers a rival framing in which groups can be vehicles of selection, and Stephen Jay Gould and Richard Lewontin attacked the view as reductionist, charging that it confuses bookkeeping, tracking which genes increase, with causation, what actually does the selecting. Many argue that gene-level and individual-level descriptions are often mathematically equivalent accounts of the same process, so the disagreement is partly about emphasis and framing rather than fact.
misreadings: Selfish is a metaphor for a gene's effect in promoting its own replication, not a claim that organisms, or people, are innately selfish, and the theory in fact explains cooperation and altruism. Reading it as licence for selfishness commits the naturalistic fallacy, deriving an ought from an is, which Dawkins explicitly rejected. The gene is not the only conceivable unit of selection, as the levels-of-selection debate makes clear. And the anthropomorphic language of genes wanting or exploiting is shorthand for selection dynamics, not a claim that genes have purposes.
origin: Set out by Richard Dawkins in his 1976 book 'The Selfish Gene', building on the gene-centred work of W. D. Hamilton, George C. Williams (notably his 1966 'Adaptation and Natural Selection'), and Robert Trivers.
